item.title: When your mockup doesn't click: what to check in Figma's code layers (free on paid plans until Nov 4)
item.description: Figma opened code layers in open beta on October 15. You can turn design frames, a GitHub repo, a website capture or a prompt into a clickable, code-backed prototype on the canvas. Checked against the release notes, help article and blog: what is confirmed and what is missing.
item.content:encoded:
A client replies to your mockup: "What happens when I press this button?" A static frame has no answer. Wiring up prototype links can eat a whole day. This is the moment you want a screen that actually responds.

On October 15, at Config India 2026, Figma opened code layers in open beta. They put prototypes backed by running code right on the canvas. This piece repeats only what I verified in Figma's release notes, help article and blog, and lists separately what remains unconfirmed.

Before you read

  • I did not run code layers for this piece. Everything below comes from official documentation.
  • The rollout is gradual, so it may not appear in your account yet. The help article says "gradually rolling out."
  • I found no supported frameworks, usage limits or per-task credit costs in the docs.
  • Plan wording differs between documents. More on that below.
  • I found no public evidence on whether the code a layer produces is good enough for production, so I don't judge that.

What a code layer is

The help article describes code layers as interactive prototypes backed by running code that sit on the canvas. Design and code live in one file, so you can compare variations side by side and push changes back to the layer.

In short, a real button sits on the canvas instead of a drawn one. Select a layer and press Play. Several layers can run at once, and you can preview on mobile through the Figma app.

Five ways to create one

MethodHow
From scratchPick the Code tool (shortcut B), drag on the canvas, then prompt the Figma agent
From your designSelect design frames and click Build selection in the right sidebar. Multiple frames work
From a GitHub repoClone a connected repository to build on an existing frontend
From a local folderUpload a folder of code files
From a websiteUse Capture code in the Figma Chrome extension, then paste into a Design file

Source: Figma Help: Code layers in Figma Design

There is one more route. You can ask a coding agent such as Claude Code to import a project into a Figma file. The docs give the example prompt "Import this project as a code layer in <Figma file URL>." Creating layers this way requires a Full seat.

Imports can be slow

The article says importing a project through MCP can take 10 minutes or more and some projects may need changes to run in a code layer. The blog says support for more complex codebases is planned. Try a small screen first.

Editing: by words, by clicking

  1. Ask the Figma agent in plain language.
  2. Open the code editor to view code, add comments and edit designs.
  3. Use the point-and-edit tool to select an element in the preview and adjust its properties. Changes apply after you click Apply in the chat.
  4. Click Reload code layer to see the result.

Step 3 stands out for designers: you can fix elements by pointing at them without reading code. How accurate it is has no public comparison.

Back to the canvas, out to GitHub

The flow isn't one-way, according to the docs.

  • Extract designs from the current state, a selected element, or a recorded flow that produces multiple frames.
  • Push updates from extracted designs back to the code layer.
  • With GitHub, Figma stores a clone you can branch, then open pull requests to merge into the original repository.

So the loop can run mockup → clickable screen → mockup → dev repo. When you hand off, you can show behavior as a running screen rather than as notes and pictures.

Who can use it, and what it costs

  • Help article: available on Education (K-12), Starter, Professional, Organization and Enterprise plans, with edit access to Figma Design files.
  • Release notes and blog: open beta, available on all plans.
  • Free period: the release notes say creating and editing within a code layer is free on paid plans through November 4. The help article says that after that date, all code layer tasks use credits.
  • Other agent work tied to the same request still uses credits.
  • Credit use varies with task complexity. No numbers are given.
  • Imports through GitHub or MCP don't use credits, but later prompts to the Make agent do.

We covered agent credits in Figma's agent started using credits. It's the same wallet, so what you'll pay after the free period can't be known from today's numbers.

Plan wording differs: the blog says all plans, while the release notes' free condition says paid plans. What a free-plan account gets can't be settled from the docs alone. Check Figma's pricing page before paying.

Admin controls are limited too. Only Enterprise plans can opt out, and admins can disable code layers only by turning off AI features altogether. Worth knowing if your team is deciding.

How it fits with the rest of that day's news

The October 15 release notes held more than code layers.

ItemStatusWhat it says
GuidelinesOpen betaAdd guidelines to published libraries so the agent follows your patterns
Code sourcesClosed betaImport GitHub repos or npm packages so the agent reflects your real design system code
Centralized design systemsPreviewBundle design libraries, code libraries and guidelines in one place
PayloadAll plansMake scaffolds a backend with CMS, database, auth and admin panel
Figma MCPAvailableFaster, more Figma products supported, 20 new partners

Source: Figma release notes, Figma blog: Config India 2026

The blog says guidelines and code sources will be available on all paid plans. Those two matter here: if code layers make a screen you can click, guidelines keep it from drifting off your rules. That ties to DESIGN.md and Figma Specs, covered earlier.

Still unconfirmed

  • Which frameworks and languages code layers support. The help article names none.
  • Per-task credit costs after the free period.
  • The quality of the code produced. I found no public evaluation.
  • Exactly what a free-plan account can do. The documents word it differently.
  • Which projects fail to import. The docs say only that some need changes.

What this means for designers

Making a prototype has meant wiring links. Code layers put "instructing a running screen in words" in that place. If people can click a design before handoff, questions like "is it supposed to move like this?" in development might shrink. That is my guess, with no verified evidence yet.

For vibe coders it runs the other way. You can bring a built screen into Figma, extract it as a design, adjust spacing and color there, and send it back. If you lack design sense, there is now a path to polish in a design tool.

What to do now

Test one small screen before November 4. Pick a login screen or a pricing table and click Build selection. When importing an outside project, avoid large ones because imports can take 10 minutes or more. A feel for how it behaves during the free window helps you judge credits later. The free window applies to paid plans.

Hand off a clickable screen with your next mockup. Instead of long notes on a static frame, show how it behaves. Start by checking whether it answers the client's one-line question: "what happens when I press this?"

Write your rules down first. Guidelines attach to published libraries. If you don't have one yet, start with a ten-line note: main color, fonts, corner radius, spacing unit. It works in any tool.

AI design tools by use are collected on AI design tools.

Summary

Figma now lets a running, code-backed prototype sit beside a static mockup, and creating and editing is free on paid plans through November 4. How far you can trust it has no public comparison yet. What is certain is that the work is moving a step from drawing a design to letting people click it.

Sources: Figma release notes, Figma Help: Code layers in Figma Design, Figma blog: Config India 2026.

item.title: When every AI-built screen looks the same, Lovable dropped its 'three design directions' step and put design systems first
item.description: Lovable removed the step that showed three design directions before the first build, and design systems are available on all paid plans. Checked against its changelog and docs: what is confirmed, what is missing, and how to set your own rules once.
item.content:encoded:
If you build screens with Lovable or Cursor, they start to look alike. Rounded cards, a familiar purple, similar spacing. Rewording the prompt doesn't change the feel much. It's easy to blame a lack of design sense and move on.

Lovable's official changelog has had a few entries on this over the past weeks. One removed the 'three design directions' step shown before a first build. Another opened design systems to every paid plan. This piece repeats only what I verified in the changelog and the official docs, and lists separately what remains unconfirmed.

Before you read

  • I did not run Lovable for this piece. Everything below comes from the changelog and the docs.
  • The changelog page is very long. I read the early part, covering entries from August to October 2026.
  • I found no public comparison showing that design systems make output look less alike. That link is my interpretation.
  • A plan description in a search summary differed from the official changelog and docs. More on that below.

What changed

The relevant changelog entries:

DateItemWhat it says
2026-08-19Design systemsAvailable on all paid plans. Attach one and every build inherits its components, tokens and design rules
2026-09-21Default design system per groupAdmins on Business and Enterprise can set a default per group
2026-10-08Design directions removedThe three directions shown before building a visually open-ended prompt are gone
2026-10-12Image edits in Files tabMark a change directly on an image; the result is saved as a new file

Source: Lovable changelog

The three directions are gone

The changelog says: "The three design directions Lovable showed before building a visually open-ended prompt have been removed." If you typed something like "make it look good" without specifying the look, Lovable used to show three directions before the first build. Now it builds the look straight from your description.

The changelog adds that Lovable still asks about color, typography and layout when your prompt leaves them open. Older chats keep the direction chosen earlier, without previews.

The changelog gives no reason for the removal, so don't read it as 'the step was useless.' All that is confirmed is that the step is gone.

Design systems on every paid plan

The August 19 entry reads: "Create a design system and attach it to your projects so every build inherits your components, tokens, and design rules." In plain terms, you define parts like buttons and cards plus color and type rules once, and later builds follow them.

Wrapping an existing npm package as a design system is Enterprise only, per the same entry. The docs make the same split: a React component library based system works on all paid plans, the npm wrapper path is Enterprise only.

What a design system looks like

Lovable's docs describe it as a way to define your component library, styling guidelines and installation instructions once and reuse them across projects in a workspace. The design system itself is a dedicated Lovable project.

The docs list three parts:

  1. Components: a React component library
  2. Schema and guidelines: a machine-readable schema of tokens, a component catalog and constraints, plus rendered docs. Lovable consults it every time it generates code
  3. Installation info: setup and required configuration

On release, the .lovable folder gets design-system.json, rules/components.md, rules/design-tokens.md and rules/library-guidelines.md. system.md is a file you write yourself and is not overwritten on release. The docs suggest putting your design philosophy and usage rules there.

That resembles the DESIGN.md approach we covered: a rules memo for the AI, kept as a file it reads each time. Lovable bundles it into the product.

How to build one

Shortened from the docs:

  1. In the prompt box's + menu, choose Design → Use a design system → Create design system. The name is used later when you attach it, so make it recognizable.
  2. Configure it in chat. Either import an existing library by npm package name or public Git URL, or build from structured instructions: goal, tech stack, components you want, and reference docs (PDF, Markdown, screenshots).
  3. Choose Release version. This generates the schema, renders docs, bumps the version and commits, so it can be attached to projects.
  4. For a new project, pick it under + → Design → Use a design system. For an existing one, use Attach design system in Project settings → General.

Once attached, components are copied to src/design-system/<slug>/ and rule files to .lovable/rules/libraries/<slug>/. When a new version appears, chat shows "Update available," and accepting it replaces the existing design system files. The docs say your project's own code is left untouched.

Limits to know first

The ones that matter most to designers, from the docs:

  • One design system per project. Remove the current one before switching.
  • An unreleased draft can't be the basis of a new project.
  • You can't convert an existing project into a design system. Create a new one.
  • Avoid editing the .lovable folder or the copied components in a connected project. Updates overwrite local edits. Make lasting changes in the design system project.
  • Detaching stops updates and rule enforcement. The copied files stay as ordinary code.
  • Only React is officially supported. Vue, Angular and Svelte are not guaranteed.
  • Reading uploaded material is best-effort, and the docs tell you to review the first output.

The plan descriptions also differ. A search summary of the docs said design systems are available on Enterprise plans. The changelog (August 19) and the docs' plan section say the React-based version is available on all paid plans. Check Lovable's pricing page before you pay.

Other changes at the same time

The October 12 entry says you can mark a change directly on an image in the Files tab by drawing over an area, pinning a comment, erasing, or removing the background. The result is saved as a new file. It follows the same direction as fixing instead of rerolling.

There was also an 'Aesthetics' update in May. Lovable's post on X says you can ask for typography, layout and color preferences, preview design concepts before building, and make bolder landing pages, apps and blogs. I got the May 11 date from the secondary outlet Create With and found no detailed Lovable doc. How it connects to the removed 'three directions' step is not confirmed in public material.

What is still unconfirmed

  • Why the three directions step was removed. The changelog gives no explanation.
  • Any public side-by-side of builds with and without a design system.
  • The credit cost of design systems. The docs say only that the setup verification step costs zero credits, and give no cost for other operations such as updates.
  • Related entries in the part of the changelog I did not read.

What it means for designers

For vibe coders the message is simple: stop persuading the tool with every prompt and attach a rule set you decided once. For designers it's a different job. Writing buttons, cards, colors and type rules in a form AI can read may become a new task. That is my guess.

If Figma Specs passes the context of a design as one markdown page, Lovable's design system looks like the coding-tool version of the same idea. Different tools, same chore: write your rules down.

So for now

Write your rules in ten lines. Pick a main color, an accent, two typefaces, a corner radius and a spacing unit. Even without Lovable, it works as a rules memo for Cursor or Claude Code. We wrote up how in the DESIGN.md piece.

Don't leave the look open in the first prompt. Per the changelog, Lovable asks when color, type and layout are unspecified. State them up front, such as "main color this, typeface this," and you skip the question.

Put the edits you like back into the rules. As the docs say, editing copied components in a connected project gets overwritten on update. Only changes made in the design system project last.

AI design tools by use are collected on the AI design tools page.

In short

Lovable removed the step that offered directions on open prompts and made design systems, which hand parts and rules to every build, a feature of all paid plans. Whether that makes screens look less alike is not confirmed. What is clear is that deciding the look is shifting from a line in a prompt to a rules file.

Sources: Lovable changelog, Lovable docs: Design systems, Lovable on X, Create With: Lovable Aesthetics.

item.title: The Figma agent used to be free to try. Now it draws AI credits: what designers should check
item.description: Figma's design agent has left beta and now consumes AI credits. Checked against Figma's FAQ and pricing page: what is confirmed, what is missing, and how to stretch a month's allowance.
item.content:encoded:
If you tried Figma's agent during the beta, you probably never worried about the cost of a prompt. That period is over. According to Figma's official AI credits FAQ, the agent in Figma Design and the Weave tools became generally available on October 6, 2026, and have consumed AI credits since.

If you don't know what a prompt costs or how large the monthly allowance is, you hit a wall at the end of the month. This piece follows Figma's FAQ, its pricing page and a community forum reply, and separates what is confirmed from what is missing.

What changed

From the 'Agent and Weave tools' section of Figma's FAQ:

  • The agent in Figma Design and the Weave tools became generally available on October 6, 2026, and now consume AI credits.
  • They share one budget with other generally available AI tools such as Figma Make.
  • Weave tools have a fixed credit cost per tool. Agent usage varies with prompt complexity, the actions taken and the context you provide.
  • Usage during the beta did not consume AI credits.
  • Organization and Enterprise admins can download a CSV of beta usage. It contains only beta-period data.

The line to notice is the shared budget. In a month when you generate a lot with Make or image tools, there is less left for the agent. The FAQ says that if other AI tools have used up the budget, the agent may show 0 credits left.

How big is a month's allowance

Here are the monthly credits listed on Figma's pricing page. Every seat gets a monthly allotment of AI credits.

PlanMonthly credits, Full seatMonthly credits, Dev and Collab seats
Starter (free)500 (150 per day, up to 500 per month)500
Professional3,000500
Organization3,500500
Enterprise4,250500

Source: Figma pricing page

On the same page, seat prices on Professional are $16 a month for Full, $12 for Dev and $3 for Collab. The page doesn't say whether the Professional prices are for monthly or annual billing. Organization is $55 for a Full seat on annual billing and Enterprise is $90. Prices can change, so check the page before you buy.

The pricing page says "Number of credits used varies by request." There is no per-feature price list. According to the FAQ, credits reset monthly and the remaining amount shows in the AI Balance menu.

What one run costs: a single clue

There is no official unit price, but there is one clue. On August 12, a post in Figma's community forum quoted a tooltip on the beta agent: "After beta, it will use 196 credits." A reply in the community described that number as a 'predictive receipt', a preview of what a similar prompt would cost after the beta. The same reply said prompts run during the beta won't be charged, now or later.

Some rough arithmetic follows. It is mine, and it rests on one prompt from one user.

  • Professional Full seat: 3,000 ÷ 196 ≈ 15 runs
  • Starter: 500 ÷ 196 ≈ 2 runs

Smaller prompts would allow more and larger ones fewer. Read it as a sense of scale, not an exact count. If you hand over whole screens every day, a month's allowance could shrink quickly. The forum answer is community guidance rather than an official policy page, and when it was written on August 12 no GA date had been set. The only reliable way to know today's cost is to run a prompt and check AI Balance.

When you run short

Teams that use AI often can buy more credits through a subscription or pay-as-you-go billing. The pricing page says purchased credits are shared by the whole team. The FAQ says that from August 25 the add-ons give more credits at the same price: 2x on Professional and 1.6x on Organization and Enterprise. It applies automatically, invoices may show adjustment lines but the net cost stays the same, and the monthly spending limit is unchanged.

What isn't confirmed

  • The average credits for one agent prompt. There is no official price list.
  • Which plans can use the agent. The pricing page doesn't say.
  • Whether seat credits pool across a team or unused credits carry over. The pricing page doesn't state it.
  • The credit ratio against other AI features such as Make and image tools.
  • The situation for the agent in FigJam and Slides. The FAQ section I checked mentions only the Figma Design agent and Weave tools.

Read it with the earlier pieces

Figma Specs was about handing context to a team and AI in one markdown page. This change adds a price to handing that context to an AI. The FAQ says credit use varies with the context you provide. Keeping your rules short might improve results and also reduce usage. That is my guess, and no public test backs it up. The rules memo is covered in the DESIGN.md piece.

So for now

Open AI Balance first. Note today's remaining credits, run one small prompt, and see how much dropped. That gives you a unit price for your own work. With no official price list, this is the most accurate method.

Split prompts into small ones. Asking for one card or one header at a time, instead of a whole screen, limits how much you spend on a result you don't like. This leans on the FAQ's note that usage varies with complexity and context.

If you're on a team, ask your admin. Purchased credits are shared, and Organization and Enterprise admins can download beta usage as a CSV. Seeing how much you used in the beta gives a rough idea of scale after GA.

AI design tools by use are collected in AI design tools.

In short

The agent started drawing credits at general availability, and there is no official price list for one run. The most reliable way is to measure your own work with AI Balance. The arithmetic here rests on a single forum number. I haven't used the agent under credit billing.

Sources: Figma Help: AI credits FAQ, Figma pricing page, Figma Community Forum: figma agent beta pricing.

item.title: Build prototypes by prompt, hand them off as code: what to check in ProtoPie MCP
item.description: ProtoPie has announced official MCP support. Studio MCP lets an AI read and edit the prototype you have open; Code MCP hands finished prototypes to coding agents. Checked against ProtoPie's own post and docs: what works and what isn't confirmed.
item.content:encoded:
ProtoPie has announced official support for MCP. The byline on ProtoPie's blog post says October 7, while the page metadata says October 15. The two dates disagree, so I couldn't confirm the exact publication date.

Anyone who has built interaction prototypes knows the scene. To make a card expand when a button is tapped, you attach a trigger, pick a response and wire up a variable. It isn't hard, but it takes many small steps. Then you hand the finished prototype to a developer and the question comes back: how do we build this behavior? ProtoPie has put AI into both of those stretches.

This piece follows ProtoPie's blog posts and docs, and separates what works from what hasn't been confirmed.

First, a disclaimer. I haven't used this feature myself. Everything below comes from what ProtoPie published. Pricing, usage limits and the exact scope per plan were either missing or inconsistent across the public pages.

What MCP does here

MCP is a convention that lets AI tools call features in other programs. In ProtoPie's docs there are two servers, and they share the same ProtoPie account.

  • Studio MCP: connects an AI to ProtoPie Studio so it can read and change the prototype you have open. It runs locally inside Studio, while the AI runs in the MCP client you connect.
  • Code MCP: lets AI coding agents take a finished prototype and rebuild it in code. It runs on your machine through npx and is read-only.

In short, one is for making and the other is for handing off.

Studio MCP: ask in words, fix by hand

The docs list five uses for Studio MCP.

  • The AI reads and edits the open prototype. It can also capture the canvas.
  • It authors layers, layouts and interactions by prompt. The example given is adding a Tap trigger to a button.
  • It uses your own component libraries, building screens from the assets and components you already have in ProtoPie.
  • It validates prototypes, checking whether behavior matches expectations and flagging interaction or flow issues.
  • It targets specific elements by ID: layers, scenes, variables, components, triggers and responses. You copy an ID and paste it into your prompt, as in Change the interaction for [element ID].

Two things stand out. First, the AI pulls real instances from your component library instead of inventing parts. Second, you point at things by ID. It reads as a way to cut down the case where you say that button and the wrong layer changes. That reading is mine, and no public test shows how accurate it is.

ProtoPie says every generated interaction stays fully editable inside Studio. You continue by hand instead of rebuilding from scratch.

Code MCP: handing a prototype to implementation

Code MCP sits on the developer side. ProtoPie says it helps AI coding agents understand finished prototypes and generate implementation output from them. The post names seven officially supported frameworks.

  • React, React Native, Qt/QML, Flutter, SwiftUI, Compose and ArkTS

Dev View, introduced alongside it, lets you share a whole prototype, a single scene, a component or one layer. Instead of telling a developer to look at the entire screen, you can narrow the context to one component.

The Figma Specs we covered passes context to coding agents through a single link too. The direction is the same, but what gets passed differs. Specs carries written context and mockups; ProtoPie carries a prototype with motion. Transitions and reactions that are hard to put into words can be shown as they are. That is my interpretation as well.

Which AI connects

ProtoPie does not ship its own model. It follows a Bring Your Own Model approach. The post bylined July 20 names MCP-compatible clients such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code and Antigravity, and says support will keep expanding. The Studio MCP docs also name Claude Desktop.

There are a few conditions.

  • ProtoPie Studio 10.3.0 or later, the version that ships the MCP server.
  • The AI client and ProtoPie Studio must run on the same computer.
  • A Pro or Enterprise plan.

The July post also says model quality matters. Models comparable to Claude Sonnet work well for simpler tasks, while Opus-class models generally produce stronger results for complex interactions and implementation. There are no numbers or test results behind this; it is ProtoPie's guidance.

A tool being connected may not be the same as getting the result you wanted. After connecting, you still decide what to ask and check what comes back. ProtoPie also assumes a flow where people fix what the AI makes.

Plans: what is confirmed and what isn't

ProtoPie's public pages describe the plans slightly differently. A table helps.

PageWhat it says
Post bylined July 20In beta; Pro and Enterprise users get it at no additional cost
October official-support postStudio MCP under MCP Core (Pro plan); Studio MCP, Code MCP and Dev View under MCP Enterprise (Enterprise plan)
Studio MCP docsPro or Enterprise plan, listed as MCP Core

Sources: ProtoPie blog: official MCP support, ProtoPie blog: from design to code, ProtoPie docs: Studio MCP

Whether Code MCP is available on the Pro plan reads differently depending on the page. The October post ties it to Enterprise, while the July post says Pro and Enterprise users pay nothing extra during the beta. It does not clearly say whether Code MCP falls inside that beta. Which one holds today is something to check on ProtoPie's pricing page. The official-support post lists no prices.

What isn't confirmed yet

  • Pricing and any AI usage limits. The official-support post has none.
  • Whether the Pro plan can use Code MCP.
  • Accuracy with Korean-language prompts. No public test exists.
  • How much you have to fix in an AI-made interaction in real work.
  • The quality of code for each of the seven frameworks.
  • The exact publication date of the official post, since dates on the page disagree.

So for now

Test it on one small interaction. A button that opens a modal is enough. If you have a Pro plan and Studio 10.3.0 or later, write down how long the same interaction takes by hand versus by prompt, and how many times you fixed it. That tells you whether it suits your team.

Tidy your component names and library first. Studio MCP pulls components from your library. Messy names confuse people and AI alike. Since you copy element IDs into prompts, keeping layer names readable helps.

Decide what you hand to developers. Whole screen or a single component? Practice narrowing it with Dev View. Rules can live in DESIGN.md or guidelines, and motion in the prototype, so each has its role.

AI design tools by use case are collected in AI design tools.

Sources: ProtoPie blog: official MCP support, ProtoPie blog: from design to code, ProtoPie docs: getting started, ProtoPie docs: Studio MCP.

item.title: Figma Specs: one markdown page that hands context to your team and to AI
item.description: Figma has put markdown documents on the canvas with Specs, now in open beta on paid plans. Checked against Figma's own post and release notes: what works, what isn't confirmed, and how it differs from DESIGN.md.
item.content:encoded:
Figma has added a feature called Specs: markdown documents that live on the canvas. It was announced at Figma's first Config event in India, and Figma's own post is dated October 15.

Open a design file and you can see the frames, but rarely why they look that way. Decisions sit in chat, requirements in a doc, mockups in Figma. Now AI agents have to read all of it too. Figma says it wants to gather that scattered context in one place on the canvas.

So this piece follows Figma's blog post and release notes rather than the launch buzz. I separate what works, who can use it, and what hasn't been confirmed.

First, a disclaimer. I haven't used this feature myself. Everything below comes from what Figma published and what news reports say. I couldn't find per-plan limits or the exact range of supported markdown syntax in anything public.

What Specs is

Figma describes Specs as a container for context that sits on the canvas. In its words, "a multiplayer container that allows context to fully express itself." Several people edit it together, and you write it in markdown.

The notable part is that designs can sit inside the document. You can embed FigJam files, frames and canvas nodes directly in a spec, so text and visuals sit side by side and you don't open a separate doc. A spec can be a standalone file or sit alongside your work on the canvas.

There are two ways to make one.

  • Drag any existing .md file onto the canvas and it becomes a spec.
  • In Figma or FigJam, press D or click the Specs icon in the toolbar to start a new one.

You can also duplicate a spec so teammates each work on their own version at the same time, then align on a direction later.

Why markdown

Markdown is easy for people to read and easy for AI to read. DESIGN.md, which we covered on October 2, uses it for the same reason: exact values like colors and type sizes go at the top, and prose below explains why and how to use them.

Specs feels like the same idea moving inside Figma, but they aren't the same thing. DESIGN.md is a file format published by Google Labs; Specs is a document on the Figma canvas. One holds rules, the other holds the context of a piece of work. You don't have to pick one. That split is my own reading.

While building this site I checked the contrast of gray text with a checker and fixed it. When the standard is written as a number, a tool points out what the eye missed. Context documents are useful in a similar way.

Agents read the spec, and comment on it

According to Figma's post, the Figma agent can read comments on a spec and reply to them, so you can work with an agent the way you would with a teammate. Separate conversations with agents run as separate threads, in parallel.

Two connectors were mentioned.

  • GitHub connector: the agent can reference a codebase and draft a technical spec.
  • Hex connector: the agent can analyze product usage data and leave the results as comments on the spec.

Coding agents connect through MCP. Paste a spec link into a coding agent's prompt, and the markdown, frame references, diagrams, code layers and Code Connect snippets come along with it. The goal is to replace "look at this Figma link and this doc" with a single link.

Figma's post includes examples too. Mark Harvey at Intuit documented an icon set's file names, categories, tags and descriptions in a spec. A Figma researcher collects brainstorm results and open questions in one. The second is closest to how designers might use it.

What shipped alongside

Here is the status of each item, from the October 15 release notes and TechCrunch.

FeatureStatusAvailability
SpecsOpen betaPaid plans
GuidelinesReleased (stage not stated)Plan not stated
Centralized design systems (design library + code library + guidelines)PreviewNot stated
Code layersPublic beta (moved from June's private beta)Not stated
Figma agentGenerally available October 6Uses AI credits

Source: Figma release notes (checked October 16), TechCrunch

Guidelines deserve attention. Per the release notes, you can attach rules, best practices and anti-patterns to a published design library as markdown files, and the agent reads them every time someone prompts with the library enabled. Our earlier piece on the week AI started drawing screens asked who holds the design rules. This is Figma's answer: people write the rules down, and the agent follows them.

Figma is also aware that AI output varies from run to run. TechCrunch reported that the announcements include tools meant to make results more predictable. No numbers on how much more predictable have been published.

The agent has used AI credits since October 6. The more context you attach and the more often you prompt, the more credits it may use, so check this if your team plans to use it. The release notes say custom skills are available even on the Starter plan.

What isn't confirmed

  • Specs pricing and when the beta ends. Figma only says open beta on paid plans.
  • Limits such as file size or number of specs.
  • Range of supported markdown syntax. You'll have to open it to see how far tables and checklists go.
  • Behavior with Korean documents. No published test shows how well the agent follows a spec written in Korean.
  • Which plans get guidelines and centralized design systems.

So for now

Drag one existing document onto the canvas as a spec. A project brief or meeting notes in .md is enough. Before writing anything new, see how what you already have looks on the canvas. If you aren't on a paid plan, you'll have to wait for access.

Write three lines on why you did it this way. Next to a mockup, note the decision, the options you dropped, and what you still don't know. These three lines are useful whether a person or an agent reads them. Keeping open questions in their own place comes from the Figma researcher's example.

Keep rules and context separate. Put colors and type in DESIGN.md or guidelines, and the background of this piece of work in the spec. They won't blur together, and it's clear which text an agent should read.

AI design tools by use are collected on AI Design Tools.

Sources: Introducing Specs: Markdown as a medium (Figma blog), Figma release notes (checked October 16), TechCrunch.

item.title: Nano Banana 2.1 is "half price". What designers should check
item.description: Google's image model Nano Banana 2.1 is out. 1K and 2K images cost half as much, but 4K doesn't, and text got better while the model card lists weak spots. Checked against Google's pricing page and model card, with charts and numbers.
item.content:encoded:
Google's image model Nano Banana has become a familiar name in Korea too. On October 6 it moved up to version 2.1.

Most launch headlines said the same thing: "4K at half price." But when I opened Google's pricing page today, only 1K and 2K were half price. 4K came down by a quarter. And the "old model shuts down October 29" line in several articles doesn't appear anywhere in Google's own docs.

So this piece follows the documents rather than the buzz. I went through Google's pricing page, model card and deprecation table one by one and kept only what designers need.

First, a disclaimer. I'm building this site with Claude Code. Every performance number below was measured by Google itself, and no one has published tests of Korean text yet.

What changed

Nano Banana 2.1 is an image generation and editing model built on Gemini 3.6 Flash. It's rolling out to the Gemini app, AI Mode in Search, AI Studio, the video tool Flow, the UI design tool Stitch and Google Ads.

Google highlighted three things: visual design, editing a region you describe in words, and consistency, so the same people and objects hold across several images. You can give it up to 14 reference images, and it tracks up to four characters and ten objects among them. Aspect ratios now stretch to long strips like 8:1, which is handy for web banners and wide signage drafts.

The smallest size, 0.5K, is gone. You now choose 1K, 2K or 4K.

Price: half at 1K and 2K, less off at 4K

The 4K price that spread at launch was $0.0756. The pricing page now says $0.113, because a 4K image uses more tokens than it did with the previous model. If you plan to generate a lot at 4K, redo the budget.

The number to notice is 2K. A 2K image on the new model ($0.050) costs less than a 1K image on the old one ($0.067). The model card explains why that matters.

Google's numbers, and the weak spots it admits

The model card reports scores from people comparing results and picking the better one. Higher means it was picked more often.

EvaluationNano Banana 2.1Nano Banana 2Nano Banana Pro
Overall preference1050990935
Infographic design1048961912
Infographic factuality0.5210.1790.265
General editing1026938939
Multi-character consistency11069781011

Source: Nano Banana 2.1 model card (October 2026). All evaluations are Google's own.

The biggest jump is infographic factuality, from 0.179 to 0.521. It gets numbers and names in charts wrong much less often. It's still far from perfect, though, so always double-check any image with figures in it.

The same model card lists weak spots. At 1K, small text often comes out blurry, and long paragraphs or page-length text are still hard. It sometimes confuses positions like left and right. It says text works "across several languages" but doesn't mention Korean.

Which brings us back to 2K. For posters or product detail images with text, generate at 2K instead of 1K. It costs less than the old model's 1K and avoids blurry small text.

Editing in words: how to ask

Choosing what to change by describing it, instead of painting a mask, is the area that improved most. Put it next to the left/right weakness, though, and how you ask starts to matter.

"The word 'SALE'" rather than "the text at top left"; "the person in the hat" rather than "the person on the right". If only one thing on screen fits the description, the model is less likely to touch the wrong spot. I covered this shift from rerolling to fixing one spot in last week's image AI piece.

Every image carries a mark

Images made with Nano Banana carry SynthID, an invisible watermark. According to reports, 2.1 also attaches Content Credentials (C2PA), which record what tool made the image. Google has a short video on how to check.

This matters for client work. If you deliver images made with Nano Banana, the client can later confirm they were AI-generated. Assume it can't be hidden and say up front where you used AI. Whether you can use the images commercially is covered in my piece on AI image commercial use.

What to try this week

Generate one Korean-language poster at 2K. Use real copy, with a title, subtitle and small print. No one has shown with numbers how well it handles Korean yet, so your own copy is the fastest test.

If you use it through the API or automations, check the model name. Google recommends 2.1 as the replacement for the previous model (Nano Banana 2), but hasn't set a shutdown date. If you've seen "shuts down October 29", check Google's deprecation table yourself. Neither model has a free API tier.

Use 4K only when you need it. Unless it's a large print image, pick drafts at 2K and render only the final one at 4K.

AI image tools by use case are under AI tools.

Sources: Nano Banana 2.1 model card, Gemini API pricing · deprecations (checked Oct 15), Neowin, Android Headlines, Apidog, Google on YouTube.

item.title: Meta's first frontier model tops a design vote. How to read that ranking
item.description: Muse Wonder, released by Meta on October 12, now ranks first for websites and UI on Design Arena, where people pick AI designs by eye. How the voting works, and what a No. 1 does and doesn't tell you, with diagrams and numbers.
item.content:encoded:
On October 12, Meta released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, its first frontier-class models since it reorganized its AI teams. The announcement was all about memory: a model that keeps track of what matters to you over days and weeks, and sticks with hard tasks until they're done.

There wasn't a word about design. But the model showed up on Design Arena the same day, and two days later it ranks first in both the Website and UI Component arenas.

Design Arena is where people look at designs made by AI and pick the better one, building a ranking from those votes. When a new model is called "No. 1 at design", this is usually where that comes from. So this time I looked first at how that ranking is made, rather than at the model itself.

First, a disclaimer. I'm building this site with Claude Code, and Anthropic's models sit on the same leaderboard. Scores shift every day as votes come in, so every number below is as of October 14.

From one vote to a ranking

Design Arena's About page explains the method in some detail. Someone types a request, like "make a landing page for a cafe", and four randomly chosen models get the same prompt at the same time. The voter sees two results side by side, without knowing which model made which, and picks one.

There are five picks in all. The first two are within pairs. In the third, the two winners meet; in the fourth, the two losers. The fifth settles the middle two places. After five picks you have a full 1st-to-4th order, and only then are the model names revealed.

These one-of-two choices are combined statistically into a score, using math similar to chess ratings. The page says every vote counts the same, with no filtering or editorial adjustment.

Unpacking "No. 1"

As of today, Muse Wonder has been in 2,086 tournaments. Here's where it finished.

It came first a little over four times in ten. In the other six, voters preferred another model's work. A No. 1 model doesn't produce the best result every time. The top of the board is also tightly packed: on another tracker, the top ten models in the Website arena sit within about 50 points of each other.

The second chart has a twist. Its highest win rate is in 3D (69%), yet it ranks only 6th there. Its lowest is Website (62%), where it ranks first. Five models in the 3D arena win more often than it does; in the Website arena, none do yet. A rank depends as much on who else is in the arena as on how good the model is.

The numbers haven't settled, either. In the first two days, its Website score moved between 1355 and 1363, and at one point it was listed second.

What the vote can't measure

Design Arena calls itself "a subjective framework" for evaluating AI design. Since it says so openly, it's worth reading the results with those limits in mind.

The prompts vary. They aren't set by the company; voters type their own. One person asks for a portfolio site, another for a game screen. There's no screening of who votes or on what device. One review pointed out that the format can reward whatever looks most striking in a few seconds.

Most of what designers weigh in real work sits outside the vote.

What a vote showsWhat a vote doesn't show
First impressionWhether it follows your brand rules
The result of a single promptWhether it holds up over two or three revisions
How finished one screen looksAccessibility, like type size and contrast
Relative ranking between modelsWhether it hands off to your files and tools

The voting method is from Design Arena's About page; the critique is from a ToolCenter review.

So the fair reading of this ranking is "the model whose first attempt caught people's eye most often". That's not nothing. First impressions matter, and these are thousands of human choices. It just doesn't mean it's the right model for your work.

Can designers use it?

For now, the direct routes are on the developer side.

WherePrice
Muse WonderMeta Model API, Muse Code$4 input, $20 output per million tokens
Muse Wonder FullHigher Muse Code subscription plansNo public per-token rate
Muse appRolling out, subscribers firstDepends on plan

Sources: Meta, TechCrunch, The Rundown. Availability varies by region and plan.

The Muse app is closer to designers. On September 29, Meta connected its Muse agent to Canva. It can pull the fonts, colors and brand assets from your Canva account to make flyers, invitations and social images, and the results stay editable in Canva. Meta says nothing publishes or sends without the user's approval. But Muse itself is only available in the US and Canada for now, and Meta hasn't said which model powers the Canva features.

The direction is clear, though. The model that just topped a design vote will soon run inside Muse, and Muse already has a hand in Canva. It's the same current as Canva, Figma and Adobe moving into ChatGPT: design tools move into chat windows, and the companies behind those chat windows have started selling their models' design sense.

Turning the leaderboard into your own judgment

Vote once yourself. Put in a request like the work you actually get, whether "an order page for a neighborhood bakery" or "an app settings screen". After five picks, when the names appear, you'll see which model your eye leans toward. That tells you more than reading the leaderboard.

Look at the arena that matches your work. Besides Website and UI Component, the site ranks Logo, Graphic Design, Slides and SVG separately. First in Website doesn't guarantee anything for logos, as Muse Wonder's 3D rank shows.

Make the final call with your own rules. The parts the vote can't measure, you have to test. Give a model one template you use often and one page of brand rules, have it build the same screen, then ask for two or three revisions. It's the same method from the Sonnet 5.5 article. If your rules are already written down, attach your DESIGN.md as is.

AI design rankings will keep flipping. This week it's Meta; next month another name may be on top. AI tools by use case are under AI tools.

Sources: Meta (Oct 12), TechCrunch, Design Arena: Muse Wonder · About (checked Oct 14), BenchLM Design Arena Website (Oct 13), ToolCenter, Canva Newsroom, Unite.AI.

item.title: When a client sends an AI draft and says "just polish this"
item.description: More clients and bosses are handing designers drafts made in ChatGPT or Claude and asking only for a finish. Rates go down while the work stays. A diagram of what's actually left, and an order you can use for quotes and conversations.
item.content:encoded:
"I roughed this out with AI. Could you just polish it up?"

Plenty of designers are getting emails like this. Attached is a logo, poster or landing page draft made in ChatGPT or Claude. And there's usually one more line: "Since it's almost done, could you bring the price down a bit?"

On October 12, Fast Company covered this. It interviewed more than a dozen graphic designers, and many described something similar over the past year and a half. Clients send AI drafts and push rates down; at work, bosses hold up AI-made screens and say "build it like this". Some designers who offered opinions were told "ask ChatGPT", and some lost jobs after being told AI could do the work. The piece described designers being turned into "pixel pushers".

First, a disclaimer. This article draws on an interview-based report and a few surveys. There's no precise statistic yet on how common this is. The diagrams and steps below are this site's summary, based on what the designers in the report described.

The "almost done" illusion

To a client, an AI draft looks close to finished. Plausible colors, plausible composition, plausible lettering. But actually using it leaves quite a lot of work.

A few points worth spelling out.

The type usually has to be set from scratch. AI-drawn lettering is a picture. You can't edit it, and non-Latin scripts break often. For a logo, it ends up being redrawn by hand.

There are no files. AI gives you one image. No layers, no vectors, no print resolution. Using it on business cards, signage and social posts is no different from making it again.

The rights check is still open. Can this image be used commercially? Does it resemble another brand's logo or a real person? That's covered in detail in Can you use AI-generated images in client work?

What the AI draft did was settle "this kind of feel". That's useful, but in the whole design job it's the front end.

Is the work actually shrinking?

It's not just a mood. Some numbers exist.

StudyWhat it looked atResult
Harvard Business School and Imperial College researchJob posts on freelance platformsWithin eight months of image AI launching, image-related posts fell about 17%
Fast Company and AIGA pricing projectAbout 1,273 freelance designers and 150 hiring managersAsked whether clients are replacing designers with AI. Detailed rate tables are paywalled
Envato State of AI in Creative Work 20261,780 creativesMost say AI is already part of their toolkit

Sources: HBR (research summary), Fast Company pricing project, Envato. Each has a different audience and questions, so they don't compare side by side.

The work that shrank was mostly simple and fast. Put the other way, the work below the waterline in the diagram, the part that needs judgment and accountability, is still a person's job. The trouble is that clients rarely see it.

How to answer a request to cut the price

"AI did most of it, so it should be cheaper" comes from pricing work by time. The image already exists, so it must take less time. So it's better to answer not with time, but with the work that's left.

What the client saysYou might answer
"It's almost done, just polish it""The direction is good. I'll show you what can be used as is and what needs rebuilding."
"AI made it, so cheaper""I'll quote by the work left, not by hours. Look at the list and drop what you don't need."
"Use this image as the logo""A logo needs to scale and clear trademark checks, so I'll redraw it based on this."
"ChatGPT said to do it this way""I'll try that direction too. Then let's put both side by side and pick."

Examples put together by this site. Adjust the tone to the situation and relationship.

The key is not to dismiss the AI draft. A client showing the direction they want as a picture is actually helpful; it's much faster than explaining in words. Just show, with a list of remaining work, that the picture is a starting point.

It's the same inside a company. When a boss holds up an AI-made screen, take it as a starting point, but separately note "what I decided from here": what you changed and why. Over time, that becomes a record that the designer did more than push pixels.

So, for now

  1. Split the lines on your quote. Instead of "design, one lot", list the remaining work line by line: rights check, resetting type, file prep, per-medium production, number of revision rounds. Clients can see what they're paying for.
  2. Ask where the draft came from. Which AI made it, and whether that service allows commercial use. Keep it in an email so the designer isn't left holding the problem later.
  3. Record what you changed. Save the original AI draft and the final work side by side. It's useful for your portfolio and for the next quote negotiation.

How AI tools are actually used on the job is in AI design tools in practice, and AI tools by use are under AI design tools.

Sources: Fast Company (Oct 12, 2026), Fast Company pricing project, HBR, Envato.

item.title: When an AI answer replaces search results, how does your brand show up?
item.description: Heathrow Airport teamed up with Adobe to measure how AI answers mention its brand. With one in four travelers reportedly turning to AI first, here's what designers working on brands should look at, with a diagram and tables.
item.content:encoded:
On October 8, London's Heathrow Airport expanded its deal with Adobe. The headline was a new website built on Adobe technology, but another part stood out: Heathrow will measure how AI like ChatGPT, Copilot and Perplexity talks about it, and look for gaps.

Adobe's reasoning: one in four consumers now turn to AI first when making travel decisions. Once people ask AI instead of typing into a search box, the "first screen" a brand has to care about changes.

First, a disclaimer. Adobe didn't publish how it arrived at the one-in-four figure. Below, I focus on where this trend meets designers' work. I'll also note that this site keeps a guide file for AI, llms.txt, to make it easier for AI to read.

Where AI answers find brands

On a search results page, logos, photos, colors and banners caught people's eyes. AI answers have almost none of that. A sentence or two of summary, one name in a recommended list, a few cited links. That's it.

And those sentences come from what the AI has read: descriptions on the official site, the alt text attached to each image, reviews and articles, and information structured for machines. However strong a brand looks visually, if its written traces are thin, it comes out blurry in AI answers.

The tool Heathrow uses

Heathrow is using Adobe's "Brand Visibility", launched in June. It does three main things.

What it does
MeasureHow often, and how accurately, the brand is mentioned on ChatGPT, Google AI Mode, Copilot and Perplexity
FindQuestions where competitors appear but you don't, and places you're described wrongly
FixSuggests which content and information to strengthen

Sources: Adobe and Heathrow, CMSWire, The Next Web. Adobe says it draws on 289 million real AI search prompts. It's enterprise software, and pricing isn't public.

That tools like this are sold to large companies means "your brand in AI answers" already has marketing budgets attached. Like search engine optimization (SEO), optimizing for AI answers is becoming its own job.

Work that lands on designers

There's a reason this can't stay a marketers-only job. Much of what AI reads passes through designers' hands.

Image descriptions (alt text). The short description attached to each image on a site. It started as an accessibility tool for people who can't see the screen, but AI reads it too. Instead of "image01.jpg" or a blank, a description of what's visible, like "Heathrow Terminal 2 departures, self-service bag drop", helps both people and AI.

The sentence that describes the brand. Logos and colors don't appear in AI answers. Instead, a sentence or two explaining "what kind of brand we are" gets quoted directly. If your brand guide has tone and manner but no single sentence describing the brand, now is the time to write one.

Page structure. AI reads pages with proper headings, subheadings, tables and lists far better. A real heading tag beats large text that only looks like a heading. That's why a design system should cover the structure of text too.

This echoes the DESIGN.md story. That was about letting AI read our design rules; this is about letting AI read our brand. Both come down to describing ourselves in text a machine can read.

So, for now

There's something you can try without big tools.

  1. Ask AI directly. Ask ChatGPT or Perplexity "what kind of place is brand X?" and "what would you recommend in field Y?". Just checking how your brand or your client is introduced, and whether anything is wrong, is a start.
  2. Fill in image descriptions first. Pick ten key images on a site you worked on and check that their descriptions aren't empty. If they are, fill them with one sentence on what's visible.
  3. Write one brand sentence. On the first page of the brand guide, write in one sentence who the brand serves and what it does. It's the sentence AI is most likely to quote.

How to hand AI your design rules is in the DESIGN.md article, and branding references are under Graphic / Branding.

Sources: Adobe and Heathrow, IT Brief UK, The Next Web, CMSWire, TechRadar.

item.title: The switch to turn off Mac AI all at once is gone. An off button is design too
item.description: macOS 27 removed the switch that turned off Apple Intelligence entirely. Users are building outside tools to strip AI out. What changed, what to check on a designer's Mac, and the question left for anyone designing AI features.
item.content:encoded:
A tool spread quietly among Mac users this week. It's called RemoveMacAI. It turns off Apple's AI features on a Mac and deletes the model files they use. Several people reported getting back more than 12GB of storage.

There's a reason a tool like this appeared. In macOS 27, released this fall, the switch that turned off all AI features at once is gone.

First, a disclaimer. I haven't run this tool on macOS 27 myself. What follows is based on reporting from Mac-focused outlets. Apple hasn't explained why it removed the switch.

What changed

Through macOS 26, there was a switch for all of Apple Intelligence. Flip it, and Writing Tools, Genmoji, Image Playground and the rest turned off, and the model files were removed.

In macOS 27, that switch is gone. You have to find and turn off each feature, and reports say the toggles are spread across several settings screens, about a dozen in all. The bigger difference is that turning them off leaves the model files in place. By Apple's own figure, that's up to 14GB on Macs with M3 or later.

RemoveMacAI fills the gap. Using a configuration-profile mechanism Apple provides for organizations, it turns features off, deletes the models and blocks them from downloading again. The developer says it doesn't touch system files directly and can be reversed. It's not a method Apple officially recommends, though.

What to check on a designer's Mac

There are two reasons designers shouldn't just skip past this.

Storage. A designer's Mac is always short on space. A few PSDs and some video sources fill it fast. Unused AI models taking 14GB is a size worth noticing.

Client material. Writing Tools rewrites selected text, and the ChatGPT extension can send content to an outside service. If you handle contracts or pre-launch material, you should at least know which features are on.

What to checkWhereWhy
Writing ToolsSystem Settings > Apple Intelligence & SiriSo you don't use it on client documents by accident
ChatGPT extensionSame placeA path for content to reach an outside service
Image Playground, GenmojiSame place (also check Screen Time)Turn off if unused
Space used by modelsSystem Settings > General > StorageSee how big the leftover model files are

Sources: MacRumors, Digital Trends, Futurism. Menu names and locations may vary by macOS version.

Using an outside tool to delete the models is your call. On a work Mac, talk to IT first; configuration profiles can clash with company management settings.

An off button is design too

This doesn't end with Mac settings. Many designers are now putting AI features into their own products. So the same question sits in front of us: when a user wants to turn this off, can they do it easily?

Apple's choice is a useful cautionary example.

  • One step to turn on, ten to turn off. It's on by default, and turning it off means visiting several screens. Users read that as "please don't turn this off."
  • What stays after you turn it off. If files remain after a feature is off, users don't trust that it's really off. So they go looking for outside tools.
  • Changes without explanation. When a switch disappears with no reason given, people assume the worst.

Do the opposite. If you design AI features, put the off controls in one place, and tell users in one line what turns off and what remains. If you change a feature, say why. If users start looking for outside tools, that's a sign the settings screen's design has failed.

So, for now

  1. Start with your own Mac. Use the table above to see which AI features are on and how much space the models use. Turn off what you don't use.
  2. Ask the same of what you build. For the AI feature you're working on, find where "off" is and count how many taps it takes. More than three is worth another look.
  3. Change with a reason. If you need to change or remove a setting, write the reason down, even as one line in the release notes.

Who sets the rules when AI draws the interface is covered in the week AI started drawing screens, and UI references are under UI/UX references.

Sources: Futurism, MacRumors, MacRumors (storage), Digital Trends, Daring Fireball.

item.title: Comments say "AI slop", surveys say yes. What Fanta's AI Halloween campaign leaves behind
item.description: Fanta's Halloween campaign, made with an AI studio, is getting slammed online. Yet consumer testing came out the other way. Who did what, why reactions split, and what designers working on brands should take from it.
item.content:encoded:
Three weeks before Halloween, one drinks campaign has become a regular topic in design media: Coca-Cola's Fanta and its "Haunted Universe".

Fanta wants to own Halloween, the way Coca-Cola calls Christmas to mind. So unlike the past two years of borrowing film characters, this year it created four monsters of its own, including a cyborg Frankenstein and a werewolf DJ. And it made them with an AI studio.

First, a disclaimer. The campaign videos are public, but there's little hard data on the reaction. For each number below, I've noted who measured it and how.

Who did what

The AI studio GRAiL produced it. A cinematic trailer came out on August 24, and the campaign then expanded to 50 markets. Fanta's account: writers, technologists, creators and artists worked together, and AI was used in the research and production phases. A human-led effort, in other words.

Ibrahim Khan, Fanta's global VP of marketing, said: "Some people think you press a few buttons and Fanta Universe pops up — it's taken us a year and a half."

Comments and numbers went opposite ways

The reaction split in two.

Online, it was mostly harsh. YouTube commenters quickly labeled the trailer "AI slop", and Creative Bloq reported that almost all comments were negative, with many vowing never to buy Fanta again. Alongside complaints that the visuals lacked polish, there was strong opposition to AI imagery itself.

The survey numbers tell another story.

When consumer research firm Zappi tested Fanta's limited Halloween products, 85% said they felt distinct, against a 71% norm, and 62% said they seemed better, against 47%. Zappi's read is that people who watched the ad itself mostly liked it and weren't very concerned with the technology behind it.

Meanwhile, in a separate July survey, 74% of Gen Z said they react negatively to AI-made marketing, and 72% said they'd taken some action against a brand because of it.

The two surveys differ in audience and questions, so neither settles it. One thing is clear, though: people quietly choosing products and people writing comments can react very differently.

Why the split?

Several things seem to overlap.

"Made with AI" came first. Fanta didn't hide its AI use. That's good, but from that moment people read every small awkwardness as AI's fault. What would have been "style" from a human becomes "because it's AI".

The characters were new. For the past two years, Fanta borrowed beloved characters like Chucky and Beetlejuice. This year's monsters are unfamiliar. Without the affection a known face brings, craft gets judged more harshly.

People watched in different places. In a survey, people watch the whole ad, then answer. In a comment section, they judge on a first impression in a few seconds. The subtle awkwardness of AI video shows more in quick first impressions.

What designers working on brands should take away

Fanta's case isn't about whether to use AI. Many brands already do, and as I noted last week, 91% of designers use AI weekly. The question is how you use it, and how you talk about it.

DecisionFanta's choiceWorth considering
Disclose AI use?YesRight call. But be specific about where it was used
Use it for what?The whole character videoBe careful where awkwardness shows, like faces and motion
What to make new?Unfamiliar charactersNew characters get judged on craft more strictly
Judge reaction by?Surveys and commentsExpect numbers and comments to disagree, from the start

Sources: Creative Bloq, eMarketer, Zappi product analysis, Zappi ad analysis, DesignRush, Marketing-Interactive.

So, for now

When a client asks "should we do this campaign with AI?", there are now some questions worth raising.

  1. Split where to use it first. Decide separately between places where awkwardness hides, like concept exploration, backgrounds and props, and places where it shows instantly, like faces and hands.
  2. Write how you'll say "made with AI" in advance. Don't hide it, but be specific: rather than "an AI ad", say "planned by people, with AI used for this part".
  3. Watch the first three seconds on their own. Beyond screening the full cut, review it like a social feed, a few seconds before scrolling past. That's where the comments come from.

Whether AI images can be used in client work is covered in Can you use AI-generated images in client work?, and graphic and branding references are under Graphic / Branding.

Sources: Creative Bloq, eMarketer, Zappi, Adweek, DesignRush, Marketing-Interactive.

item.title: Seven free "Photoshops" rebuilt with AI. Can designers switch?
item.description: A developer is building seven free, open-source apps with AI to replace Adobe's. The Photoshop replacement opens and saves PSDs but is still in early alpha. Here's where it stands and what designers should look at.
item.content:encoded:
A story made the rounds in design circles this week. A developer released seven free apps meant to stand in for Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign and Acrobat. The project is called ArtCraft, and he says he built it with AI.

Headlines everywhere said you can finally cancel Adobe. I took a calm look at whether that's true and how far along it is.

First, a disclaimer. These apps were reportedly built with Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5. I'm building this site with Claude Code from the same company. So I've leaned on what the repositories say and on other outlets' checks rather than the developer's claims. I haven't installed the apps myself.

Who, why, and how

The developer is software engineer Brandon Thomas. He says Adobe's cancellation fees were the trigger. On Adobe's "annual, paid monthly" plan, canceling before the year is up costs half of the remaining amount. The US Federal Trade Commission sued Adobe over this in 2024, and the case ended in a settlement.

Here's how it's made.

  • Written with AI. He says the code was written using Claude Opus 5.5.
  • Rebuilt from scratch in Rust. He describes it as a "clean-room" approach: not taking Adobe's code, but rebuilding from how the tools work and look.
  • Free and open source. Released under MIT and Apache 2.0, so anyone can download and modify it.

Seven apps: where they stand

Only two have reached a usable stage. PhotoCraft (Photoshop) and the Acrobat replacement are in "early alpha"; the other five are still "in development". The developer first said feature parity would come within a month, then changed that to "months, not years".

PhotoCraft opens PSDs

PhotoCraft, the furthest along, went after what matters most to designers first: the PSD. Its repository says it can open and save 8-, 16- and 32-bit PSDs, plus PSB for large files.

Of 309 public PSD test files opened and re-saved, 307 reportedly rendered correctly. The number looks high. But it's the developer's own test, and re-saved files aren't byte-identical to the originals, because the layer records and composite are rewritten.

What's missing is clear too.

In PhotoCraft today
Opening and saving PSD/PSBWorks (8, 16, 32-bit)
Generative AI featuresNone
ToolsAbout 20 missing vs. Photoshop
Type handlingStill weak
Plug-insNot supported
After Effects files (AEP)EffectCraft can't open them

Sources: PhotoCraft repository, Windows Forum, Cybernews. Early testers say it's nowhere near replacing real work yet.

Legal questions remain too. Even without copying code, an interface that looks too similar could raise "trade dress" issues, and commentators note Adobe holds many patents on how features work.

What designers should watch: the file, not the app

The takeaway for designers isn't whether you can cancel Adobe today. The answer right now is clearly no. You can't hand client work to an alpha.

There are two things worth watching instead.

First, what holds us is the file format. Designers stay with Adobe partly because the apps are good, but also because the files we trade are PSD, AI, INDD and AEP. That's why PhotoCraft put PSD compatibility first. A replacement becomes a real threat not when it has more features, but when it can open a client's file as is and send it back as is.

Second, the cost of building software is falling. One person, working with AI, put out the skeleton of seven apps. The polish is far off, but there will be more attempts like this. For Adobe, pressure on pricing and cancellation terms will likely come before pressure on features. That's not bad news for designers.

So, for now

Don't switch. Watch, and try one thing.

  1. Test with a copy of a work file. Copy a PSD you use often and open it in PhotoCraft. See which of layers, masks, adjustment layers and type layers break, and you'll get a feel for how close it is to your work. Never overwrite the original.
  2. Recheck your subscription terms. If you're on Adobe's "annual, paid monthly" plan, check when you can cancel and what the fee is. After the first year, you can generally cancel without a fee.
  3. Compare with existing free options. Long-standing free tools (GIMP, Inkscape, DaVinci Resolve and others) are still far more polished. They make a good baseline before getting excited about the new thing.

How design tools are changing in the AI era is covered in Why thirty AI drafts don't make the work any shorter, and design tools are collected under Design tools.

Sources: Cybernews, GIGAZINE, PhotoCraft repository, Windows Forum, Softonic, Engadget (FTC settlement).

item.title: The week AI started drawing screens. Who holds the design rules?
item.description: ChatGPT now answers with buttons and charts, and the Figma agent is out of beta. Two features from the same week, side by side, with diagrams on who sets the rules for the screen.
item.content:encoded:
This week brought two announcements in a row about AI drawing screens.

On October 6, Figma took its design agent out of beta. The next day, OpenAI brought GPT-6 to ChatGPT and introduced "Intelligent UI": instead of answering only in text, ChatGPT can answer with a screen that includes buttons, forms and charts. It opened to paid users first, and reaches free users starting today.

One lives in a chat window, the other inside a design tool. Different places, but in both, AI draws the screen itself. Which raises the same question: who sets the rules for that screen?

First, a disclaimer. Both features are only days old, so there are almost no hands-on reviews yet. This is based on the companies' announcements and coverage. I'll also note that I'm building this site with Claude Code.

Answers arrive as screens

OpenAI's description: GPT-6 composes answers from text, visuals and interactive elements, and decides how to lay them out for each question. Comparisons sit side by side, explanations become diagrams you can play with, and simple questions still get plain text.

OpenAI's examples: a cooking timeline next to a recipe, road-trip stops on a map, and small tools built on the spot. A savings calculator, a bill splitter, even a game you can play inside the chat.

Turn it into a designer's question and it clicks. Ask "how much should I charge per hour for freelance work?" and you used to get a few paragraphs. Now you might get sliders for hours and rate, with the estimate calculated next to them. The illustration above was drawn to show that difference.

OpenAI also shared how it works. There's a library of components OpenAI built in advance, and the model renders them onto the screen while it's still writing the answer. It doesn't wait to finish thinking; it fills in the screen as it goes. OpenAI says the model checks the interfaces it makes for clarity, usefulness and completeness, while admitting that improving its design judgment is still a work in progress.

Here's who can use it:

Details
Paid (Plus · Pro · Business · Enterprise)From Oct 7, in the Chat tab
Free · GoFrom Oct 8
Not supportedPro's thinking mode, outdated desktop apps
How to turn it off"Layout and visuals" in web settings; some visuals may still appear

Sources: OpenAI, GPT-6 and Intelligent UI for everyone, 9to5Mac, Relevant Audience. Press reports say paid plans run on GPT-6 Sol and free plans on GPT-6 Luna.

The same week, the Figma agent left beta

Figma's announcement came a day earlier. According to its October 6 release notes, the design agent is now generally available. It's faster, and you can search for Figma files and attach them during a chat. You can also watch an agent working on a teammate's request live on the canvas.

The part designers should notice is "library guidelines". You upload markdown files to a design library with rules, best practices and antipatterns, and the agent reads them every time someone prompts with that library enabled.

The free ride is over, though. From October 6, the agent uses AI credits, drawn from the same pool as Figma Make. There's no fixed price per request. Figma only says usage depends on how complex the prompt is, how many actions the agent takes and how much context you attach, like libraries or files. The agent in FigJam and Slides is still in closed beta and doesn't use credits.

Who holds the rules?

Put the two side by side and the difference is clear.

The screens ChatGPT draws are made of OpenAI's components. Whoever asks, the buttons and charts look the same. The announcement said nothing about other companies bringing their own components or design rules. OpenAI owns the rules.

The Figma agent is the opposite. It uses components your team made and reads guidelines your team wrote. Your team owns the rules. And those rules fit in a single markdown file, the same idea as DESIGN.md, which I covered last week. If you want AI to do the work, you have to write the rules down in a form AI can read.

What's left for designers

Judging when a screen beats text. OpenAI says the model decides the format for each question. That judgment is what UI designers do every day: a calculator, a table, or one sentence? OpenAI says this is still being improved, so for now a person's eye is better.

Writing the rules down. If you'll use the Figma agent, start with library guidelines. They don't need to be long. Five lines of don'ts is enough: one accent color per screen, body text never below 16px, shadows only on cards. If you already have a DESIGN.md, carry the same content over.

Watching credits for a month. More complex requests and more attached files cost more credits. For the first month, attach only what you need instead of a whole library, and count how fast the credits go.

There will only be more screens drawn by AI. Which rules they follow will come down to who writes those rules down first. AI tools by use case are under AI tools, and design system references under Design & Code.

Sources: OpenAI (Oct 7), Figma release notes (Oct 6), FourWeekMBA, 9to5Mac, Relevant Audience.

item.title: Last week, AI design tools moved toward less luck
item.description: Six AI and design stories from September 30 to October 6, on one page. The whole store, the rules, what to edit, the order of shots: what was left to luck is turning into something people decide. With numbers on how much designers use AI.
item.content:encoded:
Over the past week I posted one piece a day on AI and design: a store editor, a design rules file, two image models, a 3D printing tool, ChatGPT ads and a video model. On their own they look unrelated. Side by side, one thing stood out.

Where we used to hand everything to AI and wait for the result, people can now decide for themselves.

First, a disclaimer. This is a roundup of the past week's articles. Details and sources for each story are in the individual pieces. I'll also note that I'm building this site with Claude Code, since Claude appears in the numbers below.

Six stories on one page

Here they are again, briefly.

  • Shopify Canvas (Oct 1). Every page of a store laid out at once; click to edit, or tell the AI. From an editor that opens one page at a time to seeing the whole.
  • DESIGN.md (Oct 2). Colors, type and what not to do, written in one file for AI. I also confirmed that when rules are blank, AI fills them in on its own.
  • Ideogram 4.5 and FLUX 3 Image (Sep 30, Oct 2). Only the chosen spot changes; the rest stays. FLUX 3 sets layout with boxes first.
  • InstructMesh (Oct 1). 80% of AI-made 3D models can't be used if printed as is. Pick the flawed part and fix it in words.
  • ChatGPT image ads (Oct 5). An ad appears while your image is drawn. A new placement, and a spot where ads can slip into your references.
  • Kling 4.0 (Sep 28 onward). Ten keyframes instead of a first and last frame. You hand AI video a storyboard.
